With `?missileObjSweep=off`, bolts pass through creatures until the server impact (old behaviour). |
implementation.eye_test:
Needed (behaviour change, verifier: safe_without_eyetest=false). Boot on the 1070 with a fresh wasm (pkg rebuilt) and `?nosw=1`.
(1) Cast a war bolt at a target with another creature in the path. The bolt should explode at the first creature's surface, and `window.__projectileStops()` should show cause `client-sweep:sweepSphereAgainstObjects`.
(2) Cast at an unobstructed target. The bolt should burst at the target's surface, not 1–2 m behind it.
(3) Stand >5 m from an archer or casting monster. Its missiles should stop at your body (sweepSphereAgainstObjects rows).
(4) Run or strafe while casting bolts. There should be no "[projectile] … stopped near launch: client-sweep:sweepSphereAgainstObjects" console warnings (own-launch exemption).
(5) A/B against `&missileObjSweep=off`: bolts fly through bodies until the server impact.
Rolling Death, if available, should pass closed doors.
implementation.deviations:
- Escape flag is `?missileObjSweep=off`, per the orchestrator note. The verifier proposed `?projectileObjectSweep=off`.
- The verifier's test plan says an ETHEREAL missile skips both the door and object layers. I skip only the door layer in JS. The object layer still runs, and Rust keeps only STATIC colliders for an ETHEREAL missile. This is the exact retail obstruction_ethereal rule (FindObjCollisions :316201-316212: STATIC objects still obstruct) and matches WebAC classifyMissileObstacle. The door layer is skipped wholesale for ETHEREAL missiles because JS can't filter it per object, so a STATIC BSP object is a conservative miss there.
- The export signature is (…, radius, missileGuid, exemptLocalPlayer), with no maxRange. Rust derives its prefilter from the segment (|d| + radius, plus each object's extent in obj_collider_for_entity).
- The local-player exemption flag is decided in JS. It needs the player pose at spawn time: inst._ballisticLaunch versus _localPlayerWorldPose() at the first sweep, sticky for the flight, with an unknown pose counting as exempt.
- The JS tests are a NEW file, tests/projectile_object_sweep.test.mjs, rather than additions to projectile_visual_fidelity.test.mjs (hard rule: never edit existing tests). The visual_fidelity, ballistic_arc and spin tests run unedited and green.
- Two extra filters beyond the verifier's list:
  - Contained or no-landblock entities are skipped (they are not in the world).
  - An embedded start counts as a t=0 hit only when moving inward. Moving outward or along, it is never a hit. Without this, the swept solves' far-root exit time would read as a false hit.
implementation.follow_ups:
- Area note 1: the terrain stop runs once per frame after the substep loop. A fast bolt can tunnel through a thin ridge, and the stop snaps to gz at the overshot xy instead of the crossing point. Separate item; it lives in _tickBallisticProjectiles, which the eval-harness tests constrain.
- Area note 2: a bolt fired from indoors (or out of a doorway) never arms _ballisticTerrainOk, so it can fly through hills.
- Remote-caster self-hit: if a remote monster's interpolated body leads its server pose (it retreats while shooting), its own bolt could stop on its own body near launch. Retail had the same exposure. Watch the "stopped near launch" warnings on the 1070.
- The ETHEREAL door-layer skip also skips STATIC BSP objects (rare). A precise fix means moving BSP objects into the Rust object layer behind missile_ignore.
- The missile sweep radius is still the 0.1 m stand-in, not the missile's Setup sphere × scale.
- Optional perf: the object layer does one body lookup per world entity per substep. Add a wire-position prefilter if entity counts get very large.
- url-flags.md:1056 (projectileEnvSweep row) still says "creature cylinders need new wasm exports". Update that clause when merging the new row.

finding.title: The local player's collision body is always the human Setup: per-Setup step heights (A7-R1) are never set and the spheres are hardcoded
finding.description: Retail and ACE build the mover's transition from its own Setup: the sphere list × m_scale and step_up/step_down × scale.z. holtburger gets this right for remote movers (remote_object_info). The local player is a different story. ObjectInfo::for_local_player hardcodes the human Setup 0x02000001 body (r 0.48 spheres at z 0.475/1.35, height 1.835). The A7-R1 per-Setup step heights are read under USE_SETUP_STEP_HEIGHTS = true, but nothing writes world.player.step_up_height or step_down_height; the only assignments are the None initialisers. The field doc says the 'wasm-side Setup hydration' would fill them, and it never does. The result is that non-human heritages (Lugian, Tumerok, Undead, Gear Knight, Olthoi, Empyrean, …) and scaled players sweep with the wrong spheres, step-up and step-down. WebAC cites Olthoi 0x02001A21 step_down 0.942 and OlthoiAcid 0x02001A20 step_down 2.0 against the human 1.5; I did not verify those values against the DAT. This is more than fidelity. holtburger's own TN market-stall wedge note (transition.rs:85-98) documents what happens when the client capsule is smaller than ACE's: every UpdatePlayerPosition starts embedded on the server, fails, and the player wedges or rubber-bands. A mismatched heritage body reopens that failure. The fix is byte-identical for human characters, because Setup 0x02000001 resolves to exactly the current constants.

implementation.summary: The local player's transition body now comes from its own resident Setup, as it does in retail and ACE. `MovementSystem::transition_profile` resolves the player entity's Setup through a new `WorldState::setup_mover_body` and overwrites the capsule, radius, height and step-up/step-down. Retail-exact rules apply, per the verifier: the first min(2,n) spheres in Setup order × obj_scale, the `dummy_sphere` (r 0.1) when the Setup has no spheres (no cylsphere stand-in), step heights × scale and height = CSetup.height × scale. The pure helper is `transition::mover_body_from_setup`, returning `SetupMoverBody`, with `SetupMoverBody::HUMAN` as the fallback while the Setup is not resident. `ObjectInfo::apply_setup_body` applies it, and `scaled_setup_step_heights` is now shared with `remote_object_info`, whose behaviour is unchanged. The byte-identical claim is checked against the real client_portal.dat (light python read via tools/dat-patch/datlib.py). Setup 0x02000001 and human female 0x0200004E carry exactly the f32 bits of the PLAYER_SETUP_* / PLAYER_STEP_* consts, so every human character stays bit-identical. This is pinned by synthetic tests and by a DAT-gated test. Olthoi 0x02001A21 differs: spheres r0.65 at z0.65/1.68, step 0.942/0.942, height 2.33. OlthoiAcid 0x02001A20 also differs: r0.841 at 0.8475/2.545, step 1.3618/2.0, height 3.3795. The change is gated by a new const `USE_SETUP_PLAYER_BODY` (true) plus a wasm `?setupPlayerBody=off` runtime carrier, wired through all three live dispatch sites: arrival placement, manual slice and the simulation spine. The legacy readers `player_step_up_height` and `player_step_down_height` resolve the same Setup body, so they agree with the profile. The misleading PlayerState step-height doc is corrected; those Option fields are now an explicit override that still wins.

implementation.deviations: 1) Sphere selection is not shared with the remote path. The local player uses the verifier's retail-exact rule: first min(2,n) spheres in Setup order, and dummy_sphere when there are none. `remote_object_info` keeps its z-sort plus cylsphere fallback unchanged; only the step-height half (`scaled_setup_step_heights`) is shared, so the remote path stays byte-identical and its existing test still pins its behaviour. 2) `mover_body_from_setup` takes an extra `setup_height: Option<f32>`, the raw CSetup.height from `WorldState::setup_part_dims`, so ObjectInfo.height = CPartArray::GetHeight. When the height is unknown it falls back to the remote formula, which also gives 1.835 for the human Setup. 3) I did not write `world.player.step_*_height` each tick; there is no clean &mut hook, and doing so would fight the runtime escape. Instead the legacy readers `player_step_up_height`/`player_step_down_height` resolve the same Setup body under the const. Those readers live only on the dead legacy chain, so the runtime `=off` does not reach them. finding.title: The missile sweep skips scenery (an export already exists), tests the terrain with a point, and uses a fixed 0.1 m radius instead of the Setup sphere
finding.description: Retail moves every missile through a CTransition built from its Setup spheres × scale, so trees, boulders, outdoor statics and the terrain all stop it locally. ACE also loads landblock scenery into its server physics (Landblock.get_land_scenes), so a bolt that ACE stops on a tree trunk is still flying on holtburger's client. It explodes behind the tree a round-trip later, or at the terrain on the far side. holtburger's projectile layers leave scenery out as needing 'new wasm exports'. But `sweepSphereAgainstScenery` (precise trunk cylspheres and boulder spheres over the 3×3 landblock ring) landed in round 2 (camera-3), after physupd-1, so that part is now a JS-only change. The terrain stop fires only once the bolt's centre is 0.25 m below the terrain sample, then puts the centre on the ground, so a bolt sinks about R + 0.25 m before stopping. Every missile sweeps with a fixed 0.1 m sphere. Re-raised: round-1 physupd-1 notes listed these as wasm follow-ups. What is new is that the scenery export now exists, and WebAC has a ready combined env + heightfield design.

The terrain stop now runs every substep through a new pure helper, projectileTerrainCrossing. It probes every 0.5 m along the chord, then bisects to the first crossing, and parks the bolt there with z on the terrain surface. The 0.25 m tolerance is unchanged, and a 60 fps bolt still uses one terrain sample per frame. In the tick, the new methods are called as `this._projectileTerrainStep?.()` and `this._projectileTrackCell?.()`, and the legacy per-frame end-point test runs only when the per-substep test is off (`?projectileTerrainCrossing=off`). When the bolt leaves through an outside portal (retail CEnvCell::find_transit_cells → add_all_outside_cells, acclient.c:348250), the terrain stop arms under the spawn rule and the scenery layer joins the sweep. The terrain step runs before the env sweep and shortens the segment, so whichever contact comes first wins. No Rust edits and no new wasm exports.

finding.title: A client-side missile contact never plays the projectile's ScriptedCollision default script (the bolt's impact splash)
finding.description: On retail, a missile with ReportCollisions (0x8) and ScriptedCollision (0x8000) plays its PhysicsDesc default script at the contact point when it hits the environment (report_environment_collision) or an object (report_object_collision's AtkCollisionProfile). The PDB shows both DoCollision overloads share one body at 0058C3A0, which calls play_default_script when bit 0x8000 is set. ACE gives bolt-type spell projectiles DefaultScriptId = PlayScript.ProjectileCollision, and the Flame Bolt weenie carries PhysicsState 0x28B48 (ReportCollisions | ScriptedCollision | Inelastic | Missile). Arrows (0x20414) lack 0x8000, so this does not apply to them. holtburger correctly stopped playing this script at spawn (it is the collision script) but never plays it on collision. Its client-side stops (env sweep, terrain, and creatures once physics-collision-1 lands) show no splash; only ACE's later Explode PlayScript arrives. WebAC plays it, but only on object hits; the decomp shows environment hits play it too, so holtburger can do better than WebAC here.

finding.title: Remote root motion ignores object scale, so scaled creatures (~45% of creatures) lag or overshoot ACE and rubber-band
finding.description:
Retail and ACE multiply each frame's sequence root-motion origin by the object's m_scale while it is on walkable ground. ACE's monster movement speed is explicitly runSpeed × RunRate × ObjScale. Holtburger's default-on spine moves every remote by root_motion(), which is table speed × forward_speed, with no scale anywhere. The entity's obj_scale is used only for the collision spheres and step heights.

The LSD partial dump has 6,707 creature weenies. Of these, 3,045 have a DefaultScale more than 5% away from 1: about 1,900 at 1.25 or more, about 130 at 2.25 or more, and about 290 at 0.75 or less (e.g. Hulking Bunny 2.0, Tan Rat 2.5).

What happens to a scaled mob between ACE's 5 Hz updates:
- At scale 1.5 it dead-reckons 33% short each tick. Every update then queues an interpolation node. While the queue is active, root motion is suspended (remote_walk_gate requires !queue_active()). The body is dragged forward at 2× the unscaled adjusted max speed, which reads as stop-go.
- At scale 2 or more, the server speed (8 × run rate m/s or more) reaches or exceeds that interpolation cap. The queue never drains, nodes head-pop at 20, and the mob trails further behind with every update, arriving late and 'attacking from range'.
- Creatures at scale 0.5 overshoot twice as far and are pulled backwards 5 times a second.
- The rig's stride is scaled while JS plays a server mover's gait at forward_speed, so the feet also skate or treadmill.

The scale is wired from the wire at world/ServerObjectManager.ts:1259 `scale: data.objScale || 1,`.

- crates/holtburger-world/src/motion/root_motion.rs:126-160 `pub fn root_motion(state, table) -> RootMotion` … `velocity.y = base * state.forward_speed;` (no scale input).
- spatial/scene.rs:6634-6645 (spine walk) `spine.roots.get(&guid).map_or_else(Vector3::zero, |motion| motion.velocity)` → `body.pose.rotation.rotate_vector(v_local)`.
- scene.rs:6347-6353 (plan_remote_moves for the transition sweep) does the same.
- state/remote_movement.rs:120 `let roots = self.scene.remote_root_motions(Some(&kinematics));` builds roots with no entity scale.
- motion/remote_mover.rs:21-36: RemoteMover has radius/height but no scale field.
- spatial/remote_transition.rs:155-197 reads `e.obj_scale()` only for spheres, capsule and step heights.
- JS cadence for server movers is `scale = inst._motionSpeed` (scene3d/entities.js:10601-10631), so the gait does not compensate.

- acclient.c:319989-320025 CPhysicsObj::UpdatePositionInternal: `CPartArray::Update(v5, quantum, &offset_frame); if ( v3->transient_state & 2 ) { v6 = v3->m_scale; offset_frame.m_fOrigin.x = offset_frame.m_fOrigin.x * v6; … } else { … * 0.0 }`, then PositionManager::adjust_offset. Only the origin is scaled; omega is not.
- ACE PhysicsObj.cs:1871 `offsetFrame.Origin *= Scale;`.
- ACE WorldObject.cs:174 `PhysicsObj.SetScaleStatic(ObjScale ?? 1.0f);`.
- ACE Monster_Navigation.cs:330-339 `MoveSpeed = moveSpeed * RunRate * scale;`.
finding.proposed_change:
1. Add `pub scale: f32` (default 1.0) to RemoteMover (motion/remote_mover.rs).
2. Set it in SpatialScene::apply_remote_movement. The caller, WorldState::apply_remote_movement (state/remote_movement.rs:74-90), already has the entity: pass `entity.obj_scale()`, sanitised exactly as entity_part_dims does in state/types.rs:972-977.
3. In SpatialScene::remote_root_motions, multiply `motion.velocity` (origin only, not omega_z) by `mover.scale`. Both the floor-sampled walk and plan_remote_moves pick this up.
4. Keep the leave-ground velocity unscaled. Retail get_leave_ground_velocity uses get_state_velocity, which has no scale, so derive leave_v from the unscaled state velocity rather than the scaled walk_v.

7. Rust test in spatial::remote_spine_tests: a scale-2 RunForward@1 mover advances 8 m/s × quantum; scale 1 stays byte-identical.

finding.title: Rust remote body never takes the wire heading at rest: InterpolateTo's within-0.05 m arm drops set_heading (root cause of ?remoteSpineHeading being off)
finding.description:
When a received position is within 0.05 m of the object, retail InterpolateTo calls set_heading(target heading) unless keep_heading (IsMovingTo), then stops interpolating. Holtburger's interpolate_to returns false in that arm, with a comment that the caller does the heading snap. The only remote caller uses the return value just to decide ConstrainTo, so the heading is never written.

As a result, every at-rest UpdatePosition leaves the Rust body at whatever heading its own omega integration produced. Examples:
- a remote player stopping a turn in place (latency makes the body over- or under-rotate);
- a mob squaring up before a swing;
- an NPC or vendor facing change.

The Rust heading is not cosmetic. It sets the root-motion walk direction (`body.pose.rotation.rotate_vector`), the start of a MoveTo turn (`remote_moveto_turn_delta` from `to_heading()`), and HandleTurnToHeading's overshoot test. Under ?remoteSpineHeading it is also the drawn facing.

With the default rotation-less rows, JS draws the eased wire heading while the Rust body walks along its stale one. A remote player who turns in place and then runs therefore crab-walks sideways until the next 1 Hz node pulls it laterally.

Holtburger's own flag ledger records the symptom: ?remoteSpineHeading was turned off on 2026-10-12 because 'the Rust remote body's heading is stale at rest (not synced to the server's UpdatePosition heading)'. A grocer snapped about 96° and ended 87° off. The stated exit criterion is 'the Rust RemoteMover adopting the server's UpdatePosition heading at rest'. This arm is exactly that missing adoption.

finding.title: ConstraintManager leash never applies to remote root motion, so a remote whose positions stop runs forever (retail: 10 m, then fades out by 50 m)
finding.description:
Retail PositionManager::adjust_offset runs ConstraintManager::adjust_offset on every frame's offset, root motion included. HandleReceivedPosition re-arms ConstrainTo(object->m_position) after every MoveOrTeleport that returns 1: the teleport arm, the 96 m or more snap, and the interpolate arm, including its within-0.05 m stop. So a remote whose positions stop keeps running on its motion for 10 m (5 m indoors), then slows linearly to a halt by 50 m (20 m).

Holtburger has a correct ConstraintManager, but calls it only from step_position_head, i.e. only while an interpolation node is active. Neither the floor-sampled root-motion walk nor the transition-planned spine move ever touches it, and ConstrainTo is re-armed only when a node was queued. A remote holding a RunForward or MoveTo state with no further positions therefore runs indefinitely. This happens in three cases:
- ACE hitches: every running remote dead-reckons for the whole stall, then rubber-bands back by tens of metres, or blips past 100 m.
- Link-dead players run off until their DeleteObject.
- Remotes beyond ACE's broadcast range keep running.

In normal play the leash is nearly inert (5 Hz and 1 Hz updates reset it below 10 m), so the change is low-risk.

Related detail: holtburger picks the indoor or outdoor blip and leash distances from the target pose (`pose.is_indoors()`). Retail GetAutonomyBlipDistance and GetStart/MaxConstraintDistance read the object's own current objcell.

- adjust_offset_chain (:1275) and constrain_local_manual_delta (scene.rs:2008-2023) are local-player only.

implementation.summary:
The remote ConstraintManager leash now also applies to a remote's own (root) motion, and it re-arms after every accepted MoveOrTeleport arm. Retail does both: PositionManager::adjust_offset runs on the whole offset frame (acclient.c:388287-388304 ← UpdatePositionInternal :320027-320030), and HandleReceivedPosition re-arms after each arm (:145223-145227). So a remote whose positions stop runs 10 m at full speed (5 m indoors), then slows to a halt by 50 m (20 m). Before this change it ran on until its DeleteObject.

Changes in scene.rs:
- The remote lattice calls a new `rearm_remote_leash` (offset 0; start/max from the body's own cell after the arm, as GetStart/MaxConstraintDistance read m_position) on the hard-set, far-snap and interpolate arms, the ≤0.05 m stop included. It does not re-arm on the `!contact` arm, which returns 0 in retail.
- `plan_remote_moves` and `ground_moves` scale only the walk offset, using a new non-mutating `ConstraintManager::preview_scale`. The landing slide and the leave-ground velocity are not leashed.
- The per-body step adds the applied walk offset to the leash (`ConstraintManager::accumulate`) before the transition sweep. `RemoteMovePlan` and `ResolvedRemoteMove` carry that offset.

Changes in position_manager.rs: a new `hold_leash` mode keeps the remote leash armed after interpolation completes. Without it, the shipped auto-release would disarm it after every correction, and the run that follows would be unleashed. The hold does not include retail_leash's heading snap.

Per area note 4, the remote blip distance is also read from the body's own cell.

Everything is behind a thread-local switch, default ON, with escape `?remoteLeash=off`. It follows the motion-remote-2 convention: parsed in lib.rs and set at boot. With the flag off, every code path is byte-identical (leash factor is literally 1.0, no re-arms, no hold, no accumulation).

I checked every existing remote test by hand. All their root-motion runs stay under 10 m from the last re-arm, so the leash factor is exactly 1 there. One exception: spine_moveto_position_turns_runs_and_arrives runs 19.4 m, and its arrival time moves from about 5.55 s to about 5.9 s, which is still inside its 4–8 s window.

None of the Rust was compiled. The new JS test and the sibling remote JS tests pass.

implementation.deviations:
1) The scene step adds the already-scaled walk offset to the leash with a new `ConstraintManager::accumulate`. The verifier's step 4 said to call `constraint.adjust_offset(walk_offset, on_contact)`, but on an offset the planner already scaled that would apply the scale twice. The contact flag does not matter here: retail adds to the budget whether or not the object has contact; contact only gates the scaling.

2) Added `PositionManager::hold_leash`, which the verifier did not list. The shipped (non-retail_leash) step_queue releases the leash whenever an interpolation node completes. Without the hold, every correction that queued a node would leave the run after it unleashed, so the fix would only work after a ≤0.05 m stop or a snap. Retail keeps the leash armed (:389417). I added a separate hold rather than reusing retail_leash because retail_leash also changes the interp heading (one-frame snap), which would be a visual change.

3) Per area_missed_notes item 4, the remote blip distance in the interpolate arm is now also read from the body's own cell (GetAutonomyBlipDistance via InterpolateTo :389053 → :315861). It is behind the same flag, and `=off` keeps the target's cell.

4) When the leash has fully stopped the walk and there is no slide, the planner and the floor move produce no move. The body then stays put and is not re-exported every slice, rather than going through a zero-length transition.

5) The leash applies to every remote walk that goes through ground_moves (spine root motion, the legacy D1 state-velocity walk and the D5 MoveTo drive), since all of them are the object's own motion in retail.

6) The flag is a thread-local switch like motion-remote-2's `?remoteRestHeading`, not a scene field threaded through LoopFlags, to keep lib.rs and session edits to a minimum.

7) The Rust tests are in a new file, `spatial/remote_leash_tests.rs`, registered in spatial.rs, rather than in remote_spine_tests.rs, to avoid editing an existing test file. The helpers are copied from the spine tests (without the wire round-trip).

- A ctx-less reconcile that moves the body (EntityReplaced from a re-sent ObjectCreate) does not re-arm the leash. Retail also re-arms only in HandleReceivedPosition. Still, a runner whose leash ran out and that is then re-created stays held until its next accepted UpdatePosition. ACE re-sends positions quickly, so this is minor, but worth checking live.
- Remote sticky offsets still skip the leash, an existing documented deviation: retail runs interpolation, then sticky, then the constraint.
- area_missed_notes 2 (the leave-ground velocity uses the table walk speed, not get_state_velocity) and 3 (`SpatialSamplingConfig::max_dead_reckon` is never read) are untouched. That config could now be removed or documented as superseded by the leash.

- The orchestrator still needs to merge the url-flags.md row and the harness row, then do a wasm rebuild (release).

finding.title: Re-raise cmotiontable-2: substate links still single-hop and unsigned. WebAC adds a complete signed and via-default port with DAT-pinned human-table goldens
finding.description:
This re-raises deferred round-1 item cmotiontable-2 (logged as 'L: signed/reversed link routing + style-default double hop'). WebAC brings new evidence, listed below.

**New evidence from WebAC:**
- A second complete, compact reference: get_link with the reversed lookup, plus the GetObjectSequence reroute `if (!link || !sameSign) → link to style default + via link`, with the decomp's speed rule.
- A node player that runs links backwards and fires hooks while doing so.
- DAT-pinned goldens for the human table that can become holtburger real-data fixtures:
  - Ready→WalkForward@-0.65 plays 0x03000009 (the Walk→Ready link) backwards.
  - Dead from Run plays 0x03000007, then 0x030000C6, then 0x03000397.
  - Walk start plays 0x03000006, then 0x03000003.
  - Run start plays 0x03000005, then 0x03000002.

**Holtburger today:** it still fetches one unsigned direct link per substate change. The wasm side pins both speeds to 1.0, even though holtburger-dat's MotionTable::get_link already implements the reversed and bridge lookups.

**Visible results:**
- Each backstep start, local and remote, plays the forward Ready→Walk start link before the reversed cycle.
- A backstep stop plays Walk→Ready forwards.
- A substate change with no direct link (a sign flip, or Run→Crouch/Sit) hard-cuts instead of hopping through Ready.

finding.title: Camera fade on the local player skips held items and is lost after any re-dress (first person shows a floating weapon/torch, and the body reappears)
finding.description: Retail fades the player with CPhysicsObj::SetTranslucencyHierarchical, which recurses into the CHILDLIST, so held items fade with the body. It calls this EVERY frame in the head and inside the 0.45 m near band (CameraSet::UpdateCamera). DoObjDescChanges also re-applies the current translucency to newly swapped parts. Holtburger fades only the player's own part meshes, and it dedupes twice: per-instance (_camFadeOpacity) and per-camera (_camFadeLastOpacity). Consequences: (a) In first person, and when wall collision pulls the camera into the 0.2–0.45 m band, the body is invisible or ghosted but the wielded sword, shield, bow, wand or lit torch stays fully opaque. It hovers in front of the camera, and is plainly visible when looking down (dirZ clamp ±0.8) or during combat-stance swings. (b) Any equip, unequip or dye while in first person (or pulled in) runs _applyAppearanceHotSwap. That installs fresh, unfaded materials and leaves inst._camFadeOpacity at 0, so later pushes early-return and the player's own body renders opaque around the camera until the fade value changes. The despawn+respawn fallback has the same effect, because the camera-level dedupe never re-pushes to the new instance. (c) Minor: retail composes as max(t_cam, translucencyOriginal); holtburger multiplies opacities. WebAC's applyViewerFade traverses the whole root, held copies included, and re-clones when a mesh got new materials.
finding.webac_evidence: packages/renderer/src/scene/ViewerFade.ts:30-62 applyViewerFade: `root.visible = t < 1;` (:34), then `root.traverse((child) => {...})` over every mesh, held `wielded_*` copies included, since they hang under part nodes (models/WieldedItemVisual.ts:152-169 attachHeldChild → `part.add(itemMesh)`). It re-clones on new materials: `if (!s || (child.material !== s.faded && child.material !== s.original))` (:44-52). scene/RetailCamera.ts:113-120 cameraPlayerTranslucency (in head → 1; else the 0.45/0.2 ramp).
finding.holtburger_evidence: scene3d/entities.js:18231-18268 setLocalPlayerCameraOpacity: `if (inst._camFadeOpacity === o) return;` (:18238), then only `this._collectEntitySurfaceDids(inst, -1)`. That helper (entities.js:17977-17998) collects only `child.isMesh` direct children of each part group, but a held item is a Group mounted with `mount.add(c.root)` (entities.js:7074), so it is never faded. scene3d/camera.js:2114-2126 _applyCameraPlayerFade: `if (q === this._camFadeLastOpacity) return;` (:2116). The in-head path pushes 0 (camera.js:2017) and the near band pushes nearFadeOpacity(d) (camera.js:1635). The hot-swap replaces `inst._entityMaterials = entityMaterials` (entities.js:12751) with fresh materials and never resets _camFadeOpacity; the respawn fallback does `this.remove(g); await this.spawn(newMeta);` (entities.js:12449-12450).
finding.decomp_evidence: acclient.c:318733-318755 CPhysicsObj::SetTranslucencyHierarchical: `if (_translucency < translucencyOriginal) v6 = translucencyOriginal; ... CPartArray::SetTranslucencyInternal(v3, v6); for (i...) CPhysicsObj::SetTranslucencyHierarchical(children->objects.data[i], _translucency);`. acclient.c:149181-149216 CameraSet::UpdateCamera calls it unconditionally every frame in the head (1.0) and in the d<0.45 band. Only the ≥0.45 restore is guarded by `t > 0`. acclient.c:316853-316876 CPhysicsObj::DoObjDescChanges: after CPartArray::DoObjDescChanges, `if (translucency != 0) SetTranslucencyInternal(part_array, max(translucency, translucencyOriginal))`, so re-dressed parts keep the fade.
finding.proposed_change: In scene3d/entities.js: (1) Split the body of setLocalPlayerCameraOpacity into _applyCamFadeToInst(inst, o). Recurse it into every `inst._attachedChildren` guid (this.entityMap.get), mirroring retail's CHILDLIST walk. (2) Make the fade sticky across rebuilds. At the end of _applyAppearanceHotSwap (after `inst._entityMaterials = entityMaterials`), and in attachChildToParent when the parent's `_camFadeOpacity < 1`, re-apply the parent's current fade, resetting `_camFadeOpacity` first. For the respawn fallback, either carry `_camFadeOpacity` across, or in camera.js:2116 key the dedupe on (localGuid, an em-side appearance generation) instead of the value alone. Retail simply re-applies every frame, so dropping the camera-level dedupe in the in-head and near-band branches is also faithful; the 1/128 quantisation keeps material writes cheap. (3) Optional: compose as max(t_cam, original translucency) via the existing __preCamFadeOpacity snapshot (opacity = min(pre, 1 − t)). Escape flag `?camFadeHier=off`. Add a node test (fake rig + attached child + hot-swap) asserting the child and the swapped materials end up faded. JS-only, no wasm rebuild.

verification.reasoning:
I re-read every citation and all of them hold.

**Holtburger.** The cited lines are correct:
- `retailCamZoom` is default-ON (camera.js:607-608 `!== "off"`; url-flags.md:993), so the in-head path and near-fade are live for every user.
- `setLocalPlayerCameraOpacity` (entities.js:18231-18262) dedupes on `inst._camFadeOpacity` (:18238). It fades only DIDs from `_collectEntitySurfaceDids` (17977-17998), which walks direct `isMesh` children of `inst.parts` only.
- A held item is mounted as its own Group with `mount.add(c.root)` (entities.js:7074), so it is never faded.
- `_repointEntityMeshes` (14309) is also direct-children only.
- camera.js `_applyCameraPlayerFade` (2114-2126) dedupes on `_camFadeLastOpacity` (:2116). In-head pushes 0 (:2017); the near band pushes `nearFadeOpacity(d)` (:1635).
- `_applyAppearanceHotSwap` (12504) builds fresh part meshes and commits `inst._entityMaterials = entityMaterials` (:12751). Nothing re-applies the cam fade, and `inst._camFadeOpacity` stays stale. Because the camera-level dedupe also matches, the re-dressed body renders opaque around the camera.
- The respawn fallback (`this.remove(g); await this.spawn(newMeta)` at 12449-12450) creates a new inst that the camera dedupe never re-pushes to.
- Nothing else in the app hides held children in first person: a repo-wide grep for camFade/CameraOpacity finds only these sites.

**Decomp.**
- `SetTranslucencyHierarchical` (acclient.c:318733-318755) recurses the CHILDLIST, passing the raw `_translucency` (each object takes the max with its own `translucencyOriginal`).
- `CameraSet::UpdateCamera` (149181-149216) calls it every frame in head (1.0) and in the d<0.45 band; only the ≥0.45 restore is guarded by `t > 0`.
- `CPhysicsObj::DoObjDescChanges` (316853-316876) re-applies `max(translucency, original)` after `CPartArray::DoObjDescChanges`.

**WebAC.** `ViewerFade.ts:30-62` traverses the whole root and re-clones on new materials (:44-52). It is a usable reference, but the fix is derived from the decomp.

**Gaps.** Point (c), max vs multiply composition, is real but minor. The comparer's proposal misses one thing: an item detached from the player while faded (dropped or unwielded in first person, or pulled in near a wall) must be restored to opacity 1. Otherwise it lands on the ground invisible.

**Duplicate check.** Not a duplicate: no ledger or git entry covers hierarchical or re-dress-sticky cam fade.
verification.corrected_change:
All changes in scene3d/entities.js, JS-only, behind the escape `?camFadeHier=off`:

1. **Split the fade body.** Move the material loop of `setLocalPlayerCameraOpacity` into `_applyCamFadeToInst(inst, o)`, keeping its own per-inst dedupe and the `__preCamFadeOpacity`/`__preCamFadeDepthWrite` snapshots. `setLocalPlayerCameraOpacity(guid, opacity)` keeps that exact signature, because tests/camera_retail_math.test.cjs:270-271 regex-pins it.
2. **Recurse into children.** It applies the fade to the player, then recurses into `inst._attachedChildren` through `this.entityMap.get` (and their children, e.g. a dart on an atlatl).
3. **Make the fade sticky.** Record a manager-level `this._localCamFade = { guid, o }`. Re-apply it (after clearing `inst._camFadeOpacity`) at three points:
   - (a) the end of `_applyAppearanceHotSwap`, right after `inst._entityMaterials = entityMaterials` (~12751);
   - (b) the spawn commit when `guid === _localCamFade.guid` (covers the respawn fallback at 12449-12450 and relogs);
   - (c) `attachChildToParent` after the mount (~7074-7100), when the parent or root holder is the faded local player.
4. **Restore on detach.** In `_detachChild` (~7214), restore the child to 1 so it is not left invisible on the ground.
5. **Leave camera.js alone.** Its dedupe becomes harmless once the entity side is sticky.
6. **Optional.** Composing as max(t, original) can wait.

finding.title: World camera uses a fixed 60° vertical FOV; retail derives it from GameFOV/(aspect−0.1) with a 90° default and a Field of View option
finding.description: Retail sets the projection every frame from the Config 'Field of View' preference (m_fGameFOV, default π/2): vertical FOV = m_fGameFOV / (viewportAspect − 0.1), passed as the fovY of D3DXMatrixPerspectiveFovLH. This keeps the horizontal FOV roughly constant (~81–89°) across window shapes. Holtburger creates its PerspectiveCamera at 60° and only updates the aspect on resize, which keeps the vertical FOV constant instead. At 16:9, retail is 53.6° vertical / 84° horizontal against holtburger's 60° / 91.5°, so holtburger looks slightly fish-eyed and zoomed out. At 21:9, retail is 40.3° / 81° against 60° / 107°, a heavy edge stretch. At 4:3, retail is 73° / 89° against 60° / 75°, so holtburger is too narrow. There is also no user FOV setting. A narrower 16:9 frustum also culls more objects (a small perf gain). WebAC implements exactly the retail formula plus the option.
finding.webac_evidence: packages/renderer/src/scene/RetailCamera.ts:96-100 `export function retailVerticalFovDeg(gameFovDeg, aspect) { const rad = (gameFovDeg * Math.PI / 180) / (aspect - 0.1); if (!(rad > 0 && rad < Math.PI)) return null; ...}`. scene/SceneManager.ts:181-201 setGameFov/applyGameFov reapply it on the preference or an aspect change, keeping the previous projection on an out-of-range result.
finding.holtburger_evidence: scene3d/index.js:1583 `const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(60, cssW / cssH, 0.1, 5000);`. The resize handler at scene3d/index.js:1823-1824 only does `camera.aspect = newW / newH; camera.updateProjectionMatrix();`. There is no fov/field-of-view option in ui/graphics_settings.js or ui/camera_settings.js. The only runtime FOV writer is the camDebug helper (scene3d/camera.js:1474-1477).
finding.decomp_evidence: acclient.c:144895-144898 (SmartBox draw): `_radians = v3->m_fGameFOV / (RenderDevice::render_device->m_ViewportAspectRatio - 0.1); Render::SetFOVRad(_radians);` (same at :143950). acclient.c:145517 ctor `LODWORD(m_fGameFOV) = 1070141403` (π/2 = 90°). acclient.c:143242-143244 SetDefaultFov(degrees) stores the Config value in radians (called from :381008 on the preference change). acclient.c:378901-378913 Render::SetFOVRad rejects ≤0 or ≥π. acclient.c:453039-453048 PrimD3DRender::SetFOVInternal → `D3DXMatrixPerspectiveFovLH(&pm, _radians, m_ViewportAspectRatio, znear, zfar)` (fovY). acclient.c:382376-382392 aspect = width/height.

finding.title: ObjDesc palette recolours every surface; retail only recolours paletted surfaces of parts whose original palette equals ObjDesc.PaletteID
finding.description: Retail CPartArray::SetPalette builds the modified palette (PaletteID + Subpalettes) and applies it ONLY to parts whose CPhysicsPart::original_palette_id equals PaletteID. That id is the first of the part's surfaces with a non-zero original palette: the Surface's orig_palette_id, or the paletted texture's own palette DID set at SurfaceInitLoading. Inside a matching part, CSurface::UsePalette changes only paletted (handler 2) surfaces. Holtburger sends every surface DID of a recoloured entity (anything with paletteId≠0 or subpalettes) through fetchEntitySurfacesPixels, and Rust overrides the base palette for each one. Two consequences: (a) Fidelity: a part authored on a different palette, such as a creature accessory, armour or eye part, or a ClothingTable-swapped GfxObj whose texture palette is not the wearer's PaletteBase, gets the wearer's composite and renders wrong colours, where retail leaves it alone. (b) Efficiency and look: non-paletted (DXT/RGB) and non-matching surfaces still take the composed class. They are decoded and stored per palette signature in the paletted cache, uploaded per signature, and get no normal/height planes (composed-slim), where the plain MaterialCache path would share one material and carry holtburger's procedural normal maps. Blast radius is unmeasured: the LSD sample has 7,213 weenies with ClothingBase (recoloured on the wire), but how many have mismatching or non-paletted parts needs a DAT census. WebAC also applies the palette globally (not a lead), so this comes from the decomp. Retail's other gate (no subpalettes → no recolour) is moot on ACE, because SerializeModelData writes PaletteID only when SubPalettes.Count > 0.

verification.reasoning:
**What holds (decomp).**
- `CPartArray::DoObjDescChanges` (acclient.c:326698-326730) calls SetPalette only when `num_subpalettes > 0`.
- `CPartArray::SetPalette` (326447-326512) applies `UsePalette` only to parts whose `GetOriginalPaletteID == palID` (:326505-326506).
- `CPhysicsPart::DetermineBasePal` (314865-314889) takes the first surface with a non-zero `orig_palette_id`. It runs from SetGfxObjArray (:315287), so the value is recomputed after an AnimPartChange.
- `CSurface::UsePalette` (357769-357787) acts only when handler is 2 (4→2).
- `orig_palette_id` is read from the Surface DAT record (CSurface unpack, ~358290-358306). `CSurface::InitEnd` (358185-358192) can overwrite it with the paletted texture's own palette DID at load.
- ACE writes PaletteID only with subpalettes (WorldObject_Networking.cs:231-232) and sets it from PaletteBaseDID (:1017).

**Holtburger.** entities.js:4607-4609 / :4647, the hot-swap (12566-12568) and the Rust impl send every rig surface through the composed path with the base override. Line corrections: in the current, uncommitted src/lib.rs, `fn fetch_entity_surface_pixels_impl` is at :16161, `is_composed` at :16186, `chosen_base` at :16314, composed-slim at :16361 and the doc at :16434 (the comparer's ~ numbers are about 225 lines low).

**What is weaker than claimed.** The palette closure in `to_rgba8_clipmap` fires only for paletted textures. Non-paletted (DXT/RGB) surfaces therefore decode to the same pixels; there is no wrong colour there. The fidelity gap is limited to paletted surfaces on parts whose original palette ≠ PaletteID. Its frequency is unmeasured, and for typical human or clothing rigs (base 0x0400007E) it may be rare.

The efficiency half is real: `_paletteKey` caches per (did, palette signature) (materials.js:3991-4035), and composed-slim drops the normal planes. However, routing those surfaces to MaterialCache would ADD procedural normal maps to them, which is a visual change, not a free win.

**Gating.** A census is a hard prerequisite, and the census and any DAT-loading run are out of scope for this read-only pass.

**Duplicate check.** Not a duplicate (no original-palette work in the docs or code).

The per-part mask is also complex, because `_entityMaterials` and the paletted cache are keyed by DID, not by (part, DID).

finding.title: held-1 (deferred): WebAC has a ready held-child scale cancel, so retail's unscaled holding frame can be restored
finding.description: Re-raise of deferred held-1 (FINDINGS-round2.md:29, 'child scale inheritance changes what is drawn'), because WebAC provides a ready, tested solution, not new evidence. Retail places a held child at Frame::combine(holder part frame, holding frame). Frames carry no scale, so neither the holding offset nor the child is scaled by the holder's ObjScale or the part's DefaultScale, and the child draws at its own m_scale. Holtburger mounts the child root under the scaled part node, so it inherits the wielder's obj_scale (5229), the ScaleHook tween (17892/17898) and the non-uniform jump-squash (10920). Its comment still claims this 'matches retail'. The ledger counted about 467 scaled armed creatures in the LSD sample. WebAC divides the accumulated part→root scale out of the child's local offset and scale at attach (cancelHolderScale). When the holder's scale later changes, it rescales the outermost held copies by 1/ratio (rescaleHeldCopiesForHolder). Holtburger also has per-frame non-uniform squash, so a socket node with the scale stripped from the part's world matrix is the exact variant.

finding.title: Mouse-focused HUD widgets re-fire on Space/Enter (hotbar slot re-used on jump, Enter-to-chat swallowed); Space autorepeat scrolls the last-clicked panel
finding.description: Several HUD controls are focusable divs (tabIndex=0), and a mouse click leaves keyboard focus on them. Each has its own target-phase keydown handler that treats Enter/Space as activation. That handler does not check whether the gameplay funnel already claimed the key (ev.defaultPrevented), and does not check whether the focus came from a mouse click. Concrete failures: (a) Click a hotbar slot (potion, spell, kit), then press Space to jump. The capture-phase gameplay handler starts the jump, then the slot's own listener calls fireSlot(i) again. (b) Same state, press Enter to talk. The slot listener fires the slot and calls preventDefault, so chat-panel's document Enter-to-chat handler sees defaultPrevented and never opens chat. The player drinks a second potion instead of chatting. (c) The target-bar target (click = examine) has no ev.repeat check. Holding Space for a power jump toggles the examine floaty open and closed at the OS autorepeat rate (~30 Hz after ~500 ms). The status-indicator icons, the radar lock button (toggles UI lock) and the emote rows (re-run the emote) behave the same way. (d) Separately, index.html calls preventDefault on Space only for the non-repeat press. Holding Space for a full 1 s power jump sends ~15 autorepeat keydowns with their browser default intact, and these scroll whichever panel was last clicked (for example the chat log). Retail UI elements only take keyboard focus through explicit focus calls; clicking a shortcut does not hand it the keyboard. chat-panel.js already encodes the 'a mouse-focused tabindex must not swallow the chat key' rule, but the widgets' own handlers run before it.

Pinned by tests/verify-browser-scroll-keys.ts.
finding.holtburger_evidence: plugins/hotbar.js:1040 `el.tabIndex = 0;` and :1064-1066 `el.addEventListener("keydown", (ev) => { if (ev.key === "Enter" || ev.key === " ") { ev.preventDefault(); if (!ev.repeat) fireSlot(i); } });` (no defaultPrevented or focus-origin check). plugins/target-bar.js:414 `target.tabIndex = 0;` and :439-441 (Enter/Space → examineSelected(), no ev.repeat check; examineSelected toggles at :596-598). plugins/status-indicators.js:499 tabIndex=0, :519-524. plugins/radar.js:654 tabIndex=0, :729-732 `lockBtn.click()`. plugins/emote-panel.js:348 `row.tabIndex = 0`, :363-365 `run(entry)`. index.html:5736 `if (ev.key === " " && handle && !ev.repeat) {`: preventDefault is applied only inside this press branch (:5750), so repeats keep their default. plugins/chat-panel.js:1025-1043: onDocKeyDown returns on `ev.defaultPrevented`, so it is defeated by the widget handler, which runs earlier in the target phase.

Keyboard focus in retail is explicit, never a side effect of clicking a non-text element.
finding.proposed_change: (1) In the five widget keydown handlers (hotbar.js:1064, target-bar.js:439, status-indicators.js:519, radar.js:729, emote-panel.js:363), return early when `ev.defaultPrevented || ev.repeat`. The gameplay funnel's capture-phase handler has already claimed Space by then. (2) Add one shared rule in ui/input-funnel.js install(): a capture `click` listener that, for a pointer-originated click (ev.detail > 0) leaving document.activeElement on a non-text element inside the HUD, blurs it on the next microtask. This is retail's 'panels never take keyboard focus' rule, and it lets Enter reach the chat handler. Keyboard Tab navigation stays intact because it is not a pointer click. (3) In index.html's __gameplayKeyDown Space branch (:5736), call ev.preventDefault() for repeat keydowns too, not just the press edge, so a held power-jump never scrolls the last-clicked panel. finding.title: Movement/jump/run keys are resolved by layout-dependent ev.key instead of the physical ev.code (retail used DirectInput scan codes)
finding.description: All movement input goes through `ev.key.toLowerCase()` checked against {w,a,s,d,q,e}: the gameplay keystate, the cmdInterp edge forwarder that feeds the wasm CommandInterpreter, and camera.js's keystate mirror. ev.key is the character the active layout produces, not the physical key. Results: (a) AZERTY players get a scrambled layout (physical W position = 'z', which does nothing; physical Q = 'a' strafes). Dvorak is worse. (b) Non-Latin layouts (Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic) produce 'ц'/'ф'/... and the character cannot move at all. (c) Stuck run: if the layout changes while W is held (Alt+Shift switch), the key-up reports a different ev.key, so neither keyState.w nor the cmdInterp release edge (`__cmdInterpForward(k,false)`) fires and the interpreter keeps the WalkForward head. The input funnel's own held-key ledger already keys by ev.code because 'ev.key is not' stable, so the release ledger and the movement consumers disagree. Every rebindable action (hotbar digits, magic map, F-keys) already matches ev.code. Retail read the keyboard as DirectInput scan codes (c_dfDIKeyboard), so its keymap is positional. This is separate from the deliberate WASD/QE layout modernization (FINDINGS-round2 ruling); that default would be unchanged.

finding.title: Follow-camera right-drag free-look is not cleared on window blur and ignores ev.buttons, so the camera turns with a released mouse after Alt-Tab
finding.description: In follow mode the right-button drag state (`dragging`, `this._followDragging`) is set on canvas mousedown and cleared only by a document mouseup with button 2. If focus leaves while the button is held (Alt-Tab, a Windows toast or UAC prompt, an overlay hotkey), the page never receives that mouseup. On return, every plain mousemove (buttons=0) keeps rotating followYaw/followPitch. _followDragging stays true, which also suspends autofollow (camera.js:1191, :1317), so the camera neither follows the mouse correctly nor swings back behind the player until the user right-clicks again. The camera's onBlur only clears this.keys. The drag state is a closure local inside switchMode, so onBlur cannot reach it. WebAC drops mouse-look on blur.

finding.title: In a hidden tab, the human-session pump/tickMovement fallback runs on a throttled main-thread setInterval (once a minute after 5 min), so the movement dt exceeds HUGE_QUANTUM and is dropped
finding.description: When rAF stops (hidden or occluded tab), the only thing that keeps pumpNetFrame running in a human session is the scene3d net watchdog, a main-thread setInterval(500) with a 1 s staleness gate. pumpNetFrame drains poll_events and entity updates, and through frame_pump's stale-claim fallback it also drives handle.tickMovement. Chrome limits hidden-page timers to about 1 wake-up per second. After 5 minutes hidden it applies intensive throttling (one wake-up per minute) to chained timers once the page has been silent for 30 s. Holtburger's audio_manager deliberately ramps master gain to 0 when inactive, so the page qualifies. Effects: (a) the movement tick's dt grows to about 60 s, which the Rust spine drops entirely (dt > HUGE_QUANTUM 2.0, as in retail update_object), so server-driven MoveTo, autorun and in-flight motion freeze instead of integrating as a desktop retail client would; (b) actions that go out only after the next movement tick (casts and attacks queue a stop-completely, per the rynth/webhost.js note) and repeat-attack combat slow to one step per minute; (c) inbound events back up for a minute and then drain in one burst through the 6000-entry safety valve. Keepalive pings are fine, because the keepalive worker covers them. The bot already avoids all of this: Rynth's own Worker heartbeat calls __netFramePump when the pump is stale (200 ms hidden). Human sessions do not get the same treatment. WebAC's BackgroundTicker runs the frame step from an unthrottled worker beat whenever rAF has been silent for 250 ms.

finding.title: <ac-text> HUD labels create a new GPU-backed 2D canvas on every text change; WebAC hit IOSurface exhaustion (blank labels) with the same pattern
finding.description: Every <ac-text> render rasterises the bitmap-font string into a freshly created canvas, calls getContext('2d') with default options (accelerated), and replaces the previous canvas. Vitals, stats and chat chrome re-render often, so live and not-yet-collected canvases accumulate. WebAC found live (2026-10-03) that Chrome on macOS backs each accelerated 2D canvas with an IOSurface. When the GPU process runs out, new canvases get no backing, every label goes blank, and the compositor starves. Their fix is to default 2D contexts to CPU backing (willReadFrequently: true). A second, smaller benefit: under the HTML 2D context-loss steps, an accelerated canvas is cleared on a GPU reset. Holtburger's ac-text canvases are drawn once and never redrawn, and webgl_context_recovery.js only covers the main WebGL canvas. Labels are tiny and nearest-neighbour, so CPU raster should be pixel-identical and cheap. Holtburger already uses the CPU hint for its read-back canvases. This is lower confidence than the other findings: the failure is macOS-specific and has not been reproduced in holtburger.
finding.webac_evidence: packages/renderer/src/ui/CanvasBacking.ts:1-37: 'BUG.ui-text-blank-iosurface-exhaustion … every label goes blank … CPU-backed canvases never take an IOSurface'. It patches getContext('2d') to default `willReadFrequently: true`. Installed at boot, main.ts:409 `installCpuBacked2dCanvases();`. ui/ContextHealth.ts:1-16 counts 2D `contextlost` too.
finding.holtburger_evidence: ui/ac_font.js:466-469 renderAcText: `const canvas = document.createElement("canvas"); … const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");` (new canvas per call, default backing). By contrast scene3d/adapter.js:486/608/719 and tex_overrides.js:89 already pass `{ willReadFrequently: true }`. scene3d/webgl_context_recovery.js handles only the main WebGL canvas.

finding.title: No outbound multi-fragment send: any C2S message over 448 B is silently dropped (book pages over ~426 characters, long inscriptions)
finding.description: holtburger-session never splits an outbound message. Since the R-14 stopgap, send_message refuses any packed message larger than MAX_FRAGMENT_PAYLOAD (448 B). It logs an error and returns Ok(()), so neither the caller nor the UI ever learns the message was not sent. BookModifyPage packs guid + page + String16L(text), and with the 12-byte GameAction header that limits a page to about 426 characters. The book panel sets the textarea maxLength from the book's maxCharsPerPage, which is 1000 for 343 of the 348 LSD weenies that have the field (3 have 10000, 2 have 0). Saving any page longer than about 426 characters therefore loses the player's text without any notice. Inscribe mode removes the maxlength entirely, so long inscriptions hit the same wall. Any future large C2S message, such as retail SetCharacterOptions 0x01A1 with its PlayerModule shortcut and spell-tab lists (still commented out in opcodes.rs:489), will need fragmentation too. Retail splits every blob into 448-byte BlobFrags. ACE reassembles multi-fragment client messages by fragment sequence and only rejects a single fragment larger than 464 B, so the fix is client-only.

ClientConnection.ts:1120 calls `fragmentMessage(messageBytes, fragId, queue, fragId)`. ClientConnection.ts:1932-1960 (MAX_PACKET_FRAGMENT_BYTES = 464; sendFragmentPacket) packs at most 464 B of fragments per packet, and each packet gets its own sequence and ISAAC key. Test tests/verify-net-reliability.ts:511 'splits a large message into ≤464-byte-fragment packets, each with its own sequence and ISAAC key'.

Message dropped, session left intact"); return Ok(()); }`, then :331-338 always `count: 1, index: 0`. crates/holtburger-protocol/src/messages/transport.rs:16 `MAX_FRAGMENT_PAYLOAD: usize = 448`. crates/holtburger-protocol/src/messages/book/actions.rs:88-93 BookModifyPage packs `write_string16(buf, &self.text)`. apps/holtburger-web/plugins/book-panel.js:657-658 `const max = snap.maxCharsPerPage | 0; if (max > 0) refs.edit.maxLength = max;` and :663 inscribe mode `refs.edit.removeAttribute("maxlength")`. Tests that pin the refusal: crates/holtburger-session/src/session/tests.rs:1154-1187.
finding.decomp_evidence: acclient.c:377373 NetBlob::Fragmentize: `cTotalBlobs = bufSize / 0x1C0` (+1 for a remainder), and a loop that emits BlobFrag::CreateForSend chunks of `v8 = 448` (or the remainder). Retail always fragments at 448 B. ACE: Network/ClientPacketFragment.cs:17 rejects only `Header.Size > 464`, PacketFragment.cs:6-7 (464/448), ClientPacket.cs:14 MaxPacketSize = 1024, and NetworkSession.cs:483-530 ProcessFragment puts split fragments into partialFragments[fragment.Header.Sequence] and dispatches when Complete.
finding.proposed_change: In crates/holtburger-session/src/session/send.rs send_message, replace the refusal with retail chunking. Let count = payload.len().div_ceil(448).max(1), refused only if count > u16::MAX. For each chunk i, build a FragmentHeader with the same sequence (self.fragment_sequence) and id (self.fragment_id), count, index i, and size 16 + chunk.len(), queue unchanged. Put each fragment in its own packet: BLOB_FRAGMENTS, sequence = self.packet_sequence++, sent through the existing send_packet so the ACK piggyback, the per-packet ISAAC key (consumed in sequence order) and the retransmit cache all apply. That gives at most 20 + 4 + 464 = 488 B per datagram, well under ACE's 1024. Increment fragment_sequence and fragment_id once per message. Replace the refusal tests at tests.rs:1154-1187 with these: a 1000-character BookModifyPage gives 3 packets with consecutive sequences, one shared fragment sequence and indices 0..2, and an ACE-style reassembly of them is byte-identical to the original. Nothing to change in the netWorker proxy (it forwards GameMessages to the worker's Session). WebAC's fragmentMessage is the reference; credit WebAC (AGPL) if its code is ported.

implementation.summary: Session::send_message (crates/holtburger-session/src/session/send.rs) now splits outbound messages the way retail does instead of dropping anything over 448 B. Before, it logged an error, returned Ok and sent nothing. The new code follows NetBlob::Fragmentize (acclient.c): count = payload.len().div_ceil(448).max(1). Each message gets one fragment sequence and one id, and every fragment carries its own index and the total count. Each fragment goes in its own BLOB_FRAGMENTS packet with packet_sequence++ through the existing send_packet, so every packet gets the ACK piggyback, the next C2S ISAAC key in order and a retransmit-cache entry (at most 20+4+16+448 = 488 B per datagram). fragment_sequence and fragment_id still advance once per message, and messages of 448 B or less produce byte-identical wire output to before. finding.title: Bridge never sends ACE a Disconnect when the WebSocket ends; netWorker sessions never send one at all, so the ACE session lingers for 60 s and blocks relogin
finding.description: ACE routes client packets by header Id and only accepts them from the session's C2S endpoint. Once the browser's WebSocket is gone, the bridge's per-connection UDP socket is the only thing that can still end the ACE session. holtburger's bridge just drops that socket when any half of the connection exits. The ACE session then lives until ACE's 60 s timeout. With ACE's default account_login_boots_in_use=true, a relogin inside that window boots the old session and rejects the new login with CharacterError.Logon (the 'dropped BOTH sessions' failure described in send.rs). holtburger only avoids this on the client side, best-effort from pagehide, and only in direct mode. In ?netWorker mode, which is automatic for ?bot=1 and ?agent=1, LoopSession::Proxy::send_disconnect is a no-op. A crashed or killed tab, a closed laptop lid, a lost network between browser and bridge, or a bridge watchdog reap never send one either. WebAC's bridge sends a cleartext Disconnect from the session's own UDP socket on every close.

Test tests/verify-net-bridge.ts:147.

ARCHITECTURE.md calls the bridge a pure pipe. apps/holtburger-web/src/net_worker.rs:216-225 `LoopSession::Proxy(_) => Ok(())` with the comment '...nothing is sent from here and ACE falls back to its timeout'. apps/holtburger-web/index.html:4286-4302 pagehide calls `h.disconnect()`, best-effort. crates/holtburger-session/src/session/send.rs:384-402 records why the Disconnect matters: 'without it ACE saw the new login as "Account In Use" and dropped BOTH sessions (2026-10-09)'.
finding.decomp_evidence: Retail ends a session with a DISCONNECT (0x8000) header (what holtburger's send_disconnect already mirrors). ACE: Network/NetworkSession.cs:312-316 handles Disconnect before reordering (`session.Terminate(SessionTerminationReason.PacketHeaderDisconnect)`), and Managers/NetworkManager.cs:152 accepts a packet only `if (session.EndPointC2S.Equals(endPoint))`, so only the bridge's own socket can still do it. Handlers/AuthenticationHandler.cs:182-193 boots the old session and rejects the new one; PropertyManager.cs:501 account_login_boots_in_use defaults to true.
finding.proposed_change: Bridge, recommended: in apps/holtburger-wsbridge/src/bridge.rs, record the client id while forwarding. Either take the u16 header Id (payload bytes 12..14) of any C2S frame without CONNECT_RESPONSE whose Id is non-zero, or read the S2C ConnectRequest payload (offset 20+16). After the select! in handle_connection, whichever branch ended it, send one 20-byte cleartext Disconnect from the same UdpSocket to (target.ip, target.login_port) before dropping it: seq 0, flags 0x8000, the recorded id, checksum = Hash32 of the header with the 0xBADD70DD sentinel. For the checksum, either depend on holtburger-protocol (PacketHeader::calculate_checksum, crypto::Hash32) or add a 15-line local Hash32. Alternative that keeps the bridge AC-agnostic: after the handshake, the client registers an opaque 'last will' frame (its own cleartext Disconnect, built with build_cleartext_control_packet_bytes), and the bridge sends it on teardown. That needs a handshake v2. Client: add a TX_KIND_DISCONNECT so that in proxy mode the worker runs session.send_disconnect() instead of the no-op. A duplicate Disconnect for a session that is already gone is harmless: ACE logs it as an unsolicited packet.

implementation.summary: The bridge now ends the ACE session itself whenever a connection ends, whether by WS close, a dropped TCP link from a crashed or killed tab, a rejected frame, or a liveness-watchdog reap. After the select! in handle_connection, it sends one 20-byte cleartext DISCONNECT packet from the connection's own UDP socket to ACE's login port. The packet has seq 0, flags 0x8000, the session id, time/size/iteration 0, and checksum = Hash32 of the header with 0xBADD70DD in the checksum field. The send is bounded at 500 ms, errors are logged, and the packet is also written to the opt-in pcap capture. The session id is the low word of CConnectHeader.NetID from ACE's S2C ConnectRequest, the value retail keeps (acclient.c ClientNet::HandleConnectionRequest). A later ConnectRequest replaces it, and no Disconnect is sent before one has arrived. The AC-specific logic lives in a new pure module, apps/holtburger-wsbridge/src/disconnect.rs: local Hash32, ConnectRequest parser, packet builder and a lock-free SessionIdSlot, with unit tests plus end-to-end tests through the bridge. On the client, net_worker's outbound dispatch moved into a new natively testable module, src/net_worker_outbound.rs, which adds TX_KIND_DISCONNECT = 2. LoopSession::Proxy::send_disconnect now posts that kind instead of doing nothing. The worker runs Session::send_disconnect, posts RX_KIND_DISCONNECT and ends its wire loop, which drops the WsTransport and closes the WS, the same as direct mode's recv-loop exit. ARCHITECTURE.md no longer calls the bridge a pure pipe and gains an "Ending the ACE session" section.

finding.title: Handshake has no retransmission: one LoginRequest, one ConnectResponse after a fixed 200 ms delay, and a duplicate ConnectRequest re-keys ISAAC
finding.description: holtburger sends the LoginRequest once. It answers the ConnectRequest with one ConnectResponse, queued 200 ms later (ACE_HANDSHAKE_RACE_DELAY_MS), and never resends either. If either datagram is lost, or the ConnectResponse loses ACE's state race, login hangs: start_session documents 'No retry / timeout', and only the recv loop's 60 s or 140 s liveness checks end it. The race is real. ACE queues the ConnectRequest, then runs the password check and a synchronous DB write (UpdateLastLogin), and only after that sets State = AuthConnectResponse. ACE matches a ConnectResponse only against sessions already in that state and drops anything else silently, so a slow DB (this 8 GB laptop under swap) can take longer than the 200 ms guess. Retail resends the ConnectAck every 0.333 s, with no cap, until the server's first packet arrives, and resends the LoginRequest every 2 s up to 20 times. Separately, receive.rs runs handle_handshake_request on every ConnectRequest. A duplicate ConnectRequest datagram re-keys both ISAAC streams and resets packet_sequence to 2, which desynchronises the rest of the session. WebAC ignores a ConnectRequest that carries the current cookie and re-handshakes on a new cookie.
finding.webac_evidence: packages/network/src/ClientConnection.ts:460 `CONNECT_RESPONSE_RETRY_INTERVAL = 333; // HANDSHAKE_WAIT_FOR_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT 0.333333333 s`. :1617-1621 the resend timer runs until the first non-ConnectRequest packet (stopped at the `awaitingServerConnect` branch in handlePacket). :819-842 startLoginRetry (5 s × 4). :1576 `sameBytes(connectData.cookie, this.connectionData.connectionCookie)` returns early on a duplicate ConnectRequest. Tests tests/verify-net-reliability.ts:546, :753 ('resends the ConnectResponse every 0.333 s with no cap'), :780 and :793.
finding.holtburger_evidence: crates/holtburger-session/src/session/auth.rs:11-32: send_login_request sends once. :34-67 handle_handshake_request always runs `self.isaac_c2s = Some(Isaac::new(..)); self.isaac_s2c = ...; self.packet_sequence = 2;` and queues a single ConnectResponse at `Instant::now() + ACE_HANDSHAKE_RACE_DELAY_MS`. crates/holtburger-protocol/src/messages/transport.rs:20 `ACE_HANDSHAKE_RACE_DELAY_MS: u64 = 200`. receive.rs:469-477 calls handle_handshake_request on every ConnectRequest, with no cookie check. apps/holtburger-web/src/lib.rs:44126 '**No retry / timeout** — if ACE never responds the Promise stays pending.'
finding.decomp_evidence: acclient.c:372864-372867 ClientNet::ProcessConnection `case 4: if ( Timer::local_time - pReceiver->lastSentHandshake_ > 0.333333333 ) ClientNet::SendConnectAck(this, pReceiver);`. acclient.c:372262 ClientNet::LogonUseTime resends the LoginRequest when `(v2 - timeLastLoginRequestSent) >= 2.0` while `nRequestsSent < 20`, otherwise EndState(ID_ConnectionError_ClientTimedOutServer). ACE: Handlers/AuthenticationHandler.cs:127 EnqueueSend(connectRequest), then :229 account.UpdateLastLogin (AccountExtensions.cs:106-113, a synchronous UpdateAccount), then :232 `session.State = SessionState.AuthConnectResponse`. Managers/NetworkManager.cs:61-79 matches a ConnectResponse only when `k.State == SessionState.AuthConnectResponse` (:65). NetworkManager.cs:124-130 aborts a session that receives a LoginRequest while in AuthConnectResponse, so LoginRequest resends must stop at the first ConnectRequest.
finding.proposed_change: In holtburger-session, add a small handshake state (LoginSent{last, count} → ConnectAcked{last} → Connected) and a next_handshake_deadline() folded into the deadline min() in receive.rs recv_ordered_packet, beside the control and re-NAK deadlines. Resend the cached LoginRequest every 2.0 s, at most 20 times, until a ConnectRequest arrives, then fail with a clear error. That is retail's LogonUseTime; WebAC's 5 s × 4 is an acceptable conservative alternative. After the ConnectRequest, keep the 200 ms first send, then re-queue the cached ConnectResponse every 333 ms until the first validated S2C packet that is not a ConnectRequest moves the state to Connected. In receive.rs/auth.rs, ignore a ConnectRequest whose cookie equals connection_cookie once the handshake has started (no re-key, no sequence reset), and treat a new cookie as a fresh session. Native unit tests with a scripted transport cover: a dropped ConnectResponse recovers within 333 ms, a duplicate ConnectRequest leaves ISAAC untouched, and a dropped LoginRequest is resent after 2 s.

verification.reasoning: Code confirmed. auth.rs:11-32 sends the LoginRequest once (sequence 0, from api.rs:52). auth.rs:34-67 re-keys both ISAAC streams, sets packet_sequence=2, and queues one ConnectResponse at now+200 ms (transport.rs:20). receive.rs:469-476 calls it on every ConnectRequest. ACE gives the ConnectRequest sequence 0 (SessionConnectionData.cs:67 UIntSequence(false), then NextValue wraps to 0), so should_order_server_packet (receive.rs:217-237) does not order it, and a network-duplicated ConnectRequest would re-key. The no-retry note is at lib.rs:44394, not :44126. Retail is confirmed: ProcessConnection case 4 resends the ConnectAck after 0.333 s (acclient.c:372866-372867), and LogonUseTime resends the LoginRequest every 2 s up to 20 times (acclient.c:372262-372300). The ACE race is real: DoLogin runs as a Task (AuthenticationHandler.cs:45-46). The ConnectRequest is only enqueued (:127, NetworkSession.cs:165-175, flushed by Update), and BCrypt verify plus the synchronous UpdateLastLogin (:229) run before State=AuthConnectResponse (:232). A ConnectResponse that arrives earlier matches no session (NetworkManager.cs:61-79) and is silently lost. Resending the ConnectResponse is safe with ACE, because once AuthConnected a duplicate no longer matches. WebAC ClientConnection.ts:442-456 documents that the stuck-AuthConnectResponse hang was observed live. REFUTED part: resending the LoginRequest is unsafe against vanilla ACE whenever the server is merely slow. A second LoginRequest from the same endpoint while DoLogin #1 is in flight reaches FindOrCreateSession (same session, state AuthLoginRequest), then ProcessPacket (seq 0 bypasses the duplicate gate, NetworkSession.cs:342), then a second DoLogin. That second DoLogin hits ServerSeed==null after DiscardSeeds (:105-110), giving Terminate(BadHandshake, ServerCrash1), or it finds its own session through account_login_boots_in_use and boots it. In AuthConnectResponse it hits RemoveSession, 'Bad handshake' (NetworkManager.cs:124-130). A slow server is exactly the case the finding uses to motivate the change, while true LoginRequest loss on the WS(TCP)→loopback-UDP path is close to impossible. The JS connectTimeout (auto_login.js:125) already retries on a fresh socket, which gives a fresh ACE session. The duplicate-ConnectRequest guard is harmless but low value, since ACE sends one ConnectRequest per DoLogin. Not a duplicate.

Add a cheap guard: once ISAAC is keyed, ignore a ConnectRequest whose cookie equals connection_cookie (no re-key, no packet_sequence reset). Do NOT add LoginRequest resends against vanilla ACE. If login-loss recovery is wanted, do it as a fresh session on a new socket after a long timeout, as auto_login already does. implementation.summary: I implemented the verifier's corrected change in holtburger-session. After a ConnectRequest, the session caches the ConnectResponse (header, cookie, activation address) in a new `Session::connect_response_resend` field. The first send still goes out 200 ms later through the pending-control queue. After that, the receive loop resends it every 333 ms with no cap, as retail does in `ClientNet::ProcessConnection` case 4 (acclient.c:372867). That loop now takes the earliest of three wake-up times: pending control packets, the re-NAK timer and the new `next_handshake_deadline()`. Each resend is timed from the previous actual send: the control-packet flush calls `note_connect_response_sent`, which matches retail's `lastSentHandshake_` in `SendConnectAck`. Resending stops at the first checksum-valid server packet that is neither a ConnectRequest nor a bare cleartext ACK (retail `cs_ConnectionRequestAcked` to `cs_Connected`, acclient.c:372673). A ConnectRequest that repeats the current cookie once ISAAC is keyed is now ignored: no re-key, no `packet_sequence` reset, no new ConnectResponse and no stale TimeSync. A new cookie is still treated as a fresh handshake. I did not add LoginRequest resends; `send_login_request` documents why a second LoginRequest breaks vanilla ACE, and a test pins that it is sent once. finding.title: Server RejectRetransmit is only logged: strict in-order delivery stalls on the rejected sequence until the 300-request give-up ends the session
finding.description: When ACE can no longer resend a packet, it answers our NAK with a RejectRetransmit (an EmptyAck in retail). That happens when the packet has left ACE's 120 s retention cache. holtburger reads the list and only calls log::warn. Its receiver delivers strictly in order, so last_server_seq never moves past the rejected id. Every later packet buffers. The 0.6 s re-NAK timer asks for the gap again, ACE rejects it again (each reject is a new cleartext packet with a fresh sequence, which is itself buffered behind the gap), and after RETRANSMIT_GIVE_UP_REQUESTS = 300 (about 180 s) of a frozen world, send_request_retransmit returns Err and the recv loop disconnects. Retail removes the rejected ids from its NAK set and carries on. Retail has no strict packet-order gate at all: ProcessNewSeqNum accepts an older packet only if it is still NAKed, and dispatches each blob when it completes. The trigger is rare with vanilla ACE, because ACE keeps packets for 120 s and holtburger re-NAKs every 0.6 s, so it needs a sustained outage. When it does fire, the outcome is a 3-minute freeze and then a disconnect, where retail would lose only the messages in that packet. The fix is small and WebAC already has it (markLost).

ClientConnection.ts:1316-1321 handles a standalone RejectRetransmit before ordering ('waiting for ordering would deadlock it'). :1443-1460 acceptLostServerSeqs delivers whatever was held behind the gap. Test tests/verify-net-reliability.ts:402.

ACE: NetworkSession.cs:72 cachedPacketRetentionTime = 120 and :251 PruneCachedPackets. :283-304 queues PacketRejectRetransmit for uncached ids. Packets/PacketRejectRetransmit.cs sets `Header.Flags = PacketHeaderFlags.RejectRetransmit` (cleartext), and FlushPackets (:710+) gives it a NextValue sequence.
finding.proposed_change: In crates/holtburger-session (types.rs, receive.rs, reliability.rs), add `lost_server_seqs: BTreeSet<u32>`. In process_received_packet_metadata, which runs before ordering, insert each rejected id that is newer than last_server_seq and inside MAX_RETRANSMIT_SEQUENCE_WINDOW. In recv_ordered_packet's take_pending path, when the expected id is in the lost set, advance last_server_seq, remove the id, reset retransmit_requests_since_progress, clear highest_server_seq_seen once ordering catches up, and keep draining pending_server_packets. Make send_request_retransmit skip lost ids. A lost packet's partial fragment groups age out through the existing 256-group cap. Add native tests: a buffered N+1..N+3 behind a rejected N is delivered and no give-up fires; a reject for an id that has already arrived is ignored.

implementation.summary: A server RejectRetransmit (retail's EmptyAck) used to be only logged, so a rejected S2C id stalled ordering until the 300-request re-NAK give-up (about 180 s) ended the session. It now steps over the rejected id, as retail does (SharedNet::HandleEmptyAck, acclient.c:372177). Session has a new `lost_server_seqs: BTreeSet<u32>`. `process_received_packet_metadata` runs after the checksum check and before ordering, and it now records each rejected id that is newer than `last_server_seq`, inside MAX_RETRANSMIT_SEQUENCE_WINDOW and not already buffered. `take_pending_server_packet` first calls the new `skip_lost_server_sequences`. That moves `last_server_seq` forward without delivering anything, resets the give-up counter, clears `highest_server_seq_seen` the same way `finalize_ordered_server_packet` does, and logs the skip at warn. No ACK is sent for the skip, because the reject has its own newer sequence and its cumulative ACK covers the skipped ids. `send_request_retransmit` leaves out lost ids (and buffered ones, now including the first id) and returns `Result<bool>`. It sends nothing when no id is left to ask for, and the timer re-NAK then re-arms 600 ms out instead of spinning. A rejected id whose packet turns up before ordering reaches it is taken out of the lost set (when buffered or finalized) and delivered normally. The set stays within the reorder window, because every entry is newer than `last_server_seq` and is removed as ordering passes it. The cost of an orphaned ISAAC key in `Isaac::xors` is accepted and explained in the doc comment.

finding.title: Bridge has no admission control: listens on 0.0.0.0, relays UDP to any host:port the client names, and has no origin check or connection caps
finding.description: holtburger-wsbridge listens on 0.0.0.0:8080 by default and accepts every WebSocket upgrade without checking the Origin header. It then resolves and relays to whatever host and login/world ports the first JSON frame names: there is no target allowlist and no loopback or private-address policy. is_ace_port only compares against the ports the client supplied. There is no global or per-IP connection cap and no message or byte rate limit, and each connection gets a task and a UDP socket. As a result, any web page open in a browser that can reach the bridge (localhost, LAN or tailnet) can use it as a general UDP relay to arbitrary destinations and can exhaust its file descriptors. This is described here as a class of problem, not an exploit. ARCHITECTURE.md's 'Guards' section is stale: it still describes a CLI-configured --ace-host, but the target has been client-chosen since the per-connection handshake. Also, every bridged client reaches ACE from the bridge's IP, so an ACE MaximumAllowedSessionsPerIPAddress cap would apply to all bridged users together (it is -1 here). WebAC's bridge has a ready admission pipeline.

Per-session TokenBucket message/byte limits and abuse close in ws.on('message'). `new WebSocketServer({ ... maxPayload })`. WS ping/pong liveness every 20 s (:395-402). Pinned mode has one fixed target.

implementation.summary: holtburger-wsbridge now has admission control, modelled on WebAC's admit() (attributed). It runs in three steps. (1) At accept, connection caps apply: --max-conns (default 256) and --max-conns-per-ip (default 16). Loopback peers count only toward the global cap, because behind proxy.cjs, cloudflared or an SSH tunnel every peer is 127.0.0.1. A slot is held for the handler's whole life and freed on drop. (2) The Origin is checked in an accept_hdr_async_with_config callback and refused with a 403. Always allowed: a missing Origin (wsshim and other native clients), loopback or private-network IP-literal origins (serve.py pages, tailnet pages), and a same-host origin (Origin host equals the Host header, which covers the rotating trycloudflare host through proxy.cjs). --allow-origin adds exact origins, and `*` allows all. (3) The target allowlist runs after the JSON handshake. Ports are checked first (no DNS for a pair no entry has), then the resolved IP; a miss gets a ServerHello error naming --allow-target. The default list is localhost:9000:9001 (any loopback address) plus play.coldeve.ac:9000:9001. --allow-target HOST[:LOGIN[:WORLD]] is repeatable and replaces the list, and --allow-any-target restores the old open behaviour. Also added: a 15 s bound on the WS upgrade and on the JSON hello, so idle sockets cannot squat cap slots; a 64 KiB WS message/frame cap (tungstenite's default was 64 MiB); and an opt-in --max-frames-per-sec token bucket (burst 2x; excess frames are dropped and the connection stays up). The policy lives in the new src/admission.rs. The binary uses the new bridge::run_admitted with the policy from Cli::admission(). The existing test seams accept_loop / accept_loop_with_capture run under Admission::unrestricted(), so every existing smoke, disconnect and capture test keeps its ephemeral-port behaviour unchanged. ARCHITECTURE.md is updated: a new Admission section, rewritten Guards and CLI sections (the stale --ace-host flags are removed), the lifecycle diagram, the Auth bullet, and the local-loop recipe.
